script.opening: "Something’s not right, doctor. Over the last few months my speech has got a bit slurred — people notice — and my right hand’s gone weak and a bit wasted, with this odd twitching under the skin. I keep tripping too. The strange thing is there’s no pain at all and I can feel everything normally. What’s going on?"

facts.text: Speech slurred for about 6 months, worse when tired; his wife says he sounds "like he’s had a drink". Coughs on thin drinks like tea sometimes; food is fine. No choking episodes. (Role-player: speak with mild slurring.)

Right hand weak for 4 months — struggles with buttons and keys. The muscle between thumb and finger "has gone hollow" — will hold the hand up to the camera if asked. Twitching under the skin of the arm and calf. Right foot catches on the kerb; tripped several times, one fall, no injury.

No numbness or tingling. No pain. No neck pain. Not worse at the end of the day or after exercise in a way that recovers with rest; no droopy eyelids or double vision. Bladder and bowels normal. Breathing fine; sleeps flat on one pillow. Lost "a few pounds", not weighed.

If asked about any examination: saw a private physiotherapist 10 days ago about the tripping. "She said my foot was weak, my reflexes were very jumpy, and she could see the twitching in my calf, and told me to see you."
Well otherwise; no medicines; no allergies. Never smoked, drinks little. No family history of nerve or muscle disease. Mother died of a stroke at 80.
Married to Elaine. Retired electrical engineer; volunteers driving for a hospital transport charity. Drives every day. Two grown-up children.

Calm, precise, quietly frightened. You have looked things up and suspect something serious. If the doctor asks what you’ve been worrying about, say: "Are you talking about something like motor neurone disease?" Want honesty, not false reassurance. Become upset if the doctor seems to brush it off; settle if they are honest, kind and arrange urgent specialist assessment.

ice.ideas: "Weakness with no pain seems odd. I’ve read about these things."
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — he has privately searched online and fears motor neurone disease, which a former colleague died of. He hasn’t told Elaine how worried he is.
ice.expectations: "An honest explanation, even if it’s bad news, and to see someone quickly."

cues: "There’s no pain at all and I can feel everything normally" — purely motor pattern.
"I keep tripping" — risk of falls and the driving question.
"Are you talking about something like motor neurone disease?" — needs an honest, careful answer.

checkpoints.text: Recognises the RED-FLAG pattern of MOTOR NEURONE DISEASE — progressive, painless, purely MOTOR weakness with wasting/FASCICULATIONS, bulbar symptoms (dysarthria/dysphagia), and NO sensory loss — as highly concerning

Identifies combined UPPER and LOWER motor neurone signs from the physiotherapist’s findings and video inspection (fasciculations/wasting/weakness with brisk reflexes/upgoing plantar), assesses bulbar function (speech, swallow) and notes intact sensation

Briefly considers the differential (cervical myelopathy, multifocal motor neuropathy, myasthenia, stroke, benign fasciculations) and recognises the progressive painless motor pattern points toward MND needing specialist confirmation

Refers URGENTLY to NEUROLOGY without delay, specifying the possible diagnosis of MND in the referral letter (NICE NG42) — recognising the importance of early diagnosis, riluzole, and the multidisciplinary/respiratory/nutritional/palliative support — rather than watching and waiting

Communicates honestly that the symptoms are significant and need urgent specialist assessment WITHOUT giving him an unconfirmed life-limiting diagnosis as fact (the consultant neurologist gives the diagnosis, NG42) — avoiding both false reassurance and a definitive label
Explores his concerns, answers honestly if asked directly (acknowledging what is being looked for), and supports him compassionately through the uncertainty
Does not minimise progressive painless weakness or attribute it to a benign cause, and avoids unnecessary delay

Safety-nets and follows up: urgent neurology referral, what would warrant sooner review (rapid deterioration, choking, swallowing/breathing difficulty), driving safety and the DVLA duty if MND is diagnosed, support and a clear plan, and offer of follow-up — urgent referral with honest, compassionate handling, not premature labelling or false reassurance

worked.txt: "I’m really glad you came — these symptoms are significant and I want to take them seriously. The combination of weakness without any pain or numbness, the slurred speech, and the twitching and wasting in your hand tells me your nerves and muscles need a proper specialist assessment."

"Could you hold your right hand up to the camera for me, and then let it rest? I can see the muscle wasting and the twitching. The physiotherapist also found your reflexes very brisk, with normal feeling. Together that tells me how the nerves controlling your muscles are working in different areas."

"I’m not able to give you a firm diagnosis here today, and I don’t want to guess and frighten you or falsely reassure you. What I can say is that this pattern needs an urgent neurologist’s opinion and some nerve tests to find out exactly what’s going on."

(If he asks "is it something serious / MND?") "I can hear you’re worried, and I won’t dodge it — a condition affecting the nerves to the muscles is one of the things the specialist will be looking at and ruling in or out. That’s exactly why I want you seen quickly, so you get answers and the right support."

"I’m referring you urgently to neurology, and I’ll explain in the letter what I think needs ruling in or out, so they can see you quickly. Getting seen quickly matters — it means a proper diagnosis and, whatever it turns out to be, the right treatment and support team around you from the start."

"This is a lot to sit with, and I’m here — come back any time before the appointment. If your swallowing or breathing get noticeably worse, or you deteriorate quickly, contact us sooner. And please don’t drive if your hand or foot weakness makes it unsafe — we’ll talk about what you need to tell the DVLA once we have answers. We’ll go through whatever the specialist finds together."

f.learning: PROGRESSIVE, PAINLESS, PURELY MOTOR weakness with a MIX of upper and lower motor neurone features — muscle WASTING, FASCICULATIONS and weakness alongside brisk reflexes/spasticity/upgoing plantars — plus BULBAR symptoms (dysarthria, dysphagia) and NOTABLY no sensory loss and (early) no eye-movement or sphincter involvement, is the highly concerning red-flag pattern of MOTOR NEURONE DISEASE (MND/ALS). The painless, motor-only, progressive nature with fasciculations is the key flag. Look deliberately for combined UMN and LMN signs across regions and intact sensation (recorded findings, video inspection, or an in-person examination if not yet done), which strongly suggests MND, and briefly consider mimics (cervical myelopathy/radiculopathy — usually with sensory signs; multifocal motor neuropathy; myasthenia — fatigable, no wasting/fasciculations; stroke — sudden; benign fasciculations — no weakness/wasting). Refer URGENTLY to NEUROLOGY without delay, specifying the possible diagnosis of MND in the referral letter (NICE NG42): MND is a clinical diagnosis confirmed by a neurologist (with EMG/nerve conduction and investigations to exclude mimics), and early referral matters for timely diagnosis, disease-modifying treatment (riluzole), and access to the multidisciplinary team (respiratory/NIV, nutrition/SALT/PEG, physiotherapy, OT, communication aids, palliative care and advance care planning) — so do not watch-and-wait a progressive motor syndrome. The communication core is handling a frightening, potentially life-limiting possibility honestly but compassionately WITHOUT giving him a firm diagnosis you cannot confirm in primary care (NG42: the consultant neurologist gives the diagnosis): be honest that the symptoms are significant and need urgent specialist assessment, avoid both false reassurance and a definitive label, explore concerns, and answer honestly if the patient asks directly (acknowledging what is being looked for) while supporting him, and asking about driving (stop if symptoms make it unsafe; the DVLA must be told once MND is diagnosed).

knowledge.summary: Progressive, painless, purely motor weakness with wasting, fasciculations and bulbar symptoms is MND until a neurologist says otherwise. Look for mixed upper and lower motor neurone signs with normal sensation (on video and in any recorded examination; arrange a face-to-face neurological examination if it would change the plan, without delaying referral), refer without delay naming the possible diagnosis, and be honest if he asks, without giving a firm diagnosis.

points.t: Progressive painless weakness, muscle wasting, fasciculations, slurred speech, swallowing difficulty, foot drop or tripping, with no sensory loss. Eye movements and sphincters are usually spared early. A mix of lower motor neurone signs (wasting, fasciculations, weakness) and upper motor neurone signs (brisk reflexes, spasticity, upgoing plantars) across different regions is characteristic.

Cervical myelopathy or radiculopathy (usually with sensory signs or neck pain), multifocal motor neuropathy, myasthenia gravis (fatigable, no wasting or fasciculations), stroke (sudden onset), thyroid disease, and benign fasciculations (no weakness or wasting). The neurologist confirms the diagnosis, usually with neurophysiology and tests to exclude mimics.

NG42 [1]: if you suspect MND, refer the person without delay, and specify the possible diagnosis in the referral letter. Contact the consultant neurologist directly if you think the person needs to be seen urgently. Routine blood tests can be done at the same time but should not delay the referral.

NG42 [1]: information about the diagnosis, prognosis and management should be given by a consultant neurologist with experience of MND, unless it is clinically necessary to give it urgently. Provide information and support throughout the diagnostic process, especially during uncertainty.

Care is coordinated by a specialist multidisciplinary team: respiratory assessment and non-invasive ventilation, nutrition and gastrostomy decisions, speech and language therapy and communication aids, physiotherapy, occupational therapy, and palliative care with advance care planning [1]. Riluzole is recommended by NICE TA20 [2] and started by a specialist.

Ask about choking, chest infections, weight loss, breathlessness lying flat, morning headaches and daytime sleepiness, which suggest bulbar or respiratory involvement needing faster action. Falls and hand weakness affect safety at home and in the car. Once MND is diagnosed, he must tell the DVLA [3].

Who can come with him, driving, worry, practical support.
Video observation of wasting, fasciculations, tongue and speech, plus the physiotherapist’s recorded UMN and LMN signs; further examination never delays referral.
MND versus cervical myelopathy, myasthenia, multifocal motor neuropathy, stroke and benign fasciculations.
Screened for choking, weight loss, chest infections and respiratory symptoms.
Stated that the pattern is serious and neurological without giving a diagnosis he cannot confirm.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time

Clear triggers for faster review; follow-up after neurology; support offered.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options

ro.d: Picked up swallowing and “no pain at all” as significant cues and explored them.
Idea (something serious), concern (a serious cause), expectation (an explanation, even bad news).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.

model.text: Hello Mr Pereira, I’m Dr Ahmed. Thanks for joining on video. What’s been happening?

Something’s not right, doctor. Over the last few months my speech has got a bit slurred, people notice. My right hand’s gone weak and a bit wasted, with this odd twitching under the skin. I keep tripping too. The strange thing is there’s no pain at all and I can feel everything normally. What’s going on?

Thank you for explaining it so clearly. You’ve noticed a lot of changes, and I can hear it’s unsettling. I’d like to ask a few questions and look at a few things on the camera, and after that I’ll tell you honestly what I think. Is that okay?
model.why: Structures the consultation and promises honesty

model.text: Yes, please.
Has it come on gradually, or were there sudden changes at any point?
Gradually. Bit by bit over months.
Does the weakness get worse as the day goes on or with repeated use, and better with rest? Any double vision or drooping eyelids?
No, it’s the same all day. My eyes are fine.
Any neck pain, or pins and needles or numbness anywhere? Any problems with your bladder or bowels?
model.why: Screens for myelopathy and sphincter involvement

model.text: None of that.
You mentioned swallowing. Do you cough or choke when you eat or drink?
Sometimes with drinks, I have to be careful.
Have you lost weight, had chest infections, or felt breathless lying flat, or woken with headaches?
model.why: Screens for nutritional and respiratory involvement

model.text: I haven’t weighed myself. Breathing seems fine.
Could you hold both hands up to the camera, then rest them still on the table? And stick your tongue out for me and leave it resting in your mouth.

The muscles in your right hand look thinner, and I can see the twitching you described. Your speech sounds slurred to me too. The physiotherapist also found weakness at your right ankle, twitching in your calf and brisk reflexes, with normal feeling. I don’t want anything to hold up getting you to a specialist.
model.why: Looks for combined UMN and LMN signs; confirms intact sensation

model.text: Is that good or bad?
Before I answer, what have you been thinking it might be?
I’ve been worried it’s something serious. Weakness with no pain just seems odd. It’s been on my mind constantly.
I’m sorry you’ve been carrying that on your own. What were you hoping to get from today?
An explanation. Even if it’s bad news.

I’ll be honest with you. The pattern you have, weakness and thinning of muscles with twitching, slurred speech, and no pain or numbness, points to a problem with the nerves that control the muscles, rather than a trapped nerve or anything in the joints. It isn’t something I can diagnose here. It needs a neurologist, and I want you seen urgently.
model.why: Honest about significance; no premature label; urgent referral

model.text: Are you talking about something like motor neurone disease?

I won’t dodge that. Motor neurone disease is one of the conditions the neurologist will be looking for, and I’ll say so in my letter. There are other conditions that can look like this, and some are treatable, so I can’t tell you it is MND. What I can promise is that you’ll be seen quickly and not left waiting in the dark.
model.why: Answers a direct question honestly without confirming an unconfirmed diagnosis

model.text: That’s a lot to take in.
It is. Take a moment. Would you like me to go over anything again, or is there someone you’d like with you when you see the specialist?
I’ll bring someone. What happens next?

I’ll refer you to the neurologist today and phone them to ask for an urgent appointment. They’ll do nerve tests and other checks. Whatever it turns out to be, early specialist care means treatment and support start sooner. In the meantime, take small sips and sit upright to drink, and with the tripping and your hand, please don’t drive until the specialist has seen you and advised.
model.why: Urgent neurology with direct contact (NG42); practical safety

model.text: Okay. I’ll get lifts.

If you start choking on food, get chest infections, feel short of breath, or things get worse quickly, contact us straight away. Book to see me after the neurology appointment and we’ll go through what they found together. Can you tell me what we’ve agreed?
Urgent neurologist, you’ll phone them. Careful with drinks, no driving for now, and come back if swallowing or breathing get worse.
Exactly. I’m here if anything comes up before then.

social.t: He has been worrying on his own. Offer to include someone he trusts, and give him a way to reach the practice before the appointment.
Hand weakness and tripping affect work, driving and safety at home; occupational therapy and physiotherapy will be part of specialist care.

legal.t: Once MND is diagnosed, he must tell the DVLA; Group 1 drivers may keep driving if safe control is maintained, with licences reviewed periodically (DVLA). Until assessed, advise him not to drive if weakness affects safe control.
If MND is confirmed, advance decisions to refuse treatment and lasting power of attorney (Mental Capacity Act 2005) should be discussed early, while he can communicate easily.

professional.t: GMC Decision making and consent (2020) supports sharing information patients want. Answer direct questions honestly, and let the neurologist confirm the diagnosis (NG42).
Offer a follow-up after the neurology appointment, and code the suspected diagnosis so colleagues know the context.

community.t: The MND Association offers information and support for people being investigated, as well as after diagnosis.

redFlags: Choking on food or drink, weight loss, chest infections
Breathlessness lying flat, morning headaches, daytime sleepiness
psychosocial: Worry and how he is coping
Work, driving and safety at home
ice: Idea: something serious, since weakness without pain seems odd
Concern: fear of a serious cause
Expectation: an explanation, even if it is bad news

playbook.diagnosis: “The weakness, muscle thinning and twitching, with slurred speech and no pain or numbness, point to a problem with the nerves that control the muscles. It needs a neurologist urgently to find the cause.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Think of the nerves to your muscles as electrical wiring from the brain and spinal cord. The wiring for movement seems affected, while the wiring for feeling is working normally. A specialist needs to test the wiring to find out why.”

management.reflectIce: “You wanted an honest explanation. This is serious enough that I want a specialist to see you quickly, and I’ll tell them exactly what we’re looking for.”
management.psychosocial: Offer support, invite someone to the appointment, and advise on driving and swallowing safety.
sharedPlan: Neurology referral today naming the possible diagnosis, plus a phone call for urgency (NG42)
Routine bloods if needed, without delaying referral
safetyNet: Contact the practice at once for choking, chest infection, breathlessness or rapid worsening

pitfalls.intro: This station tests whether you recognise a red-flag pattern without the usual cancer signs, and whether you can be honest under uncertainty. Candidates fail by reassuring, by delaying, or by announcing a diagnosis they cannot confirm.

items.fail: Attributing the symptoms to a trapped nerve, age or anxiety.
items.why: Progressive painless motor weakness with fasciculations and bulbar symptoms is a red flag.
items.fix: Name the pattern and refer urgently.

items.fail: Ordering tests and reviewing in a month before referring.
items.why: NG42: refer without delay; tests must not hold up referral.
items.fix: Refer today and phone the neurologist.

items.fail: Skipping the swallow and breathing questions.
items.why: Choking and respiratory weakness need faster action.
items.fix: Ask about choking, weight, chest infections, orthopnoea and morning headaches.

items.fail: Dodging the direct question about MND.
items.why: Evasion breaks trust and increases fear.
items.fix: “It’s one of the things being looked for. I can’t confirm it, and you’ll be seen quickly.”

items.why: NG42: the diagnosis should come from a neurologist, and mimics exist.
items.fix: Be honest about seriousness, not certain about the label.

items.why: Hand weakness and tripping affect safe driving and falls.
items.fix: Advise no driving until assessed, and DVLA notification if diagnosed.

Gradual versus sudden, fatigability, eyes, sensory and sphincter symptoms, choking, weight, breathing.
Mixed UMN and LMN signs, tongue, sensation. What he fears and wants.
A serious nerve problem needing urgent neurology; if asked about MND, say it is being looked for, without confirming.
Referral today plus phone call, swallow safety, driving, safety-net, follow-up after neurology.

wordPics.fail: Reassures that it is probably a trapped nerve or age; routine referral or watch and wait; or announces “you have MND” as fact; avoids the question when he asks directly.
wordPics.pass: Recognises the progressive painless motor pattern, looks for UMN and LMN signs on video and arranges an examination, refers urgently to neurology, and is honest that it is serious.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: rules out mimics in the history; asks about swallow and breathing; answers the direct question honestly without confirming; names the possible diagnosis in the referral and phones the neurologist; allows silence; gives swallow and driving advice; arranges follow-up.

avoid.dont: “It’s probably just a trapped nerve in your neck.”
avoid.instead: “The weakness with no pain or numbness needs a neurologist to look at it urgently.”
avoid.why: False reassurance delays diagnosis and support.

avoid.dont: “I’m afraid you have motor neurone disease.”
avoid.instead: “MND is one of the things the neurologist will be looking for. I can’t confirm it here.”
avoid.why: NG42: the diagnosis should be given by a neurologist, and mimics must be excluded.
Evasion when asked directly breaks trust.

NG42 [1]: if you suspect MND, refer the person without delay, and specify the possible diagnosis in the referral letter. Contact the consultant neurologist directly if you think the person needs to be seen urgently. Routine blood tests can be done at the same time but should not delay the referral.

NG42 [1]: information about the diagnosis, prognosis and management should be given by a consultant neurologist with experience of MND, unless it is clinically necessary to give it urgently. Provide information and support throughout the diagnostic process, especially during uncertainty.

Care is coordinated by a specialist multidisciplinary team: respiratory assessment and non-invasive ventilation, nutrition and gastrostomy decisions, speech and language therapy and communication aids, physiotherapy, occupational therapy, and palliative care with advance care planning [1]. Riluzole is recommended by NICE TA20 [2] and started by a specialist.

Ask about choking, chest infections, weight loss, breathlessness lying flat, morning headaches and daytime sleepiness, which suggest bulbar or respiratory involvement needing faster action. Falls and hand weakness affect safety at home and in the car. Once MND is diagnosed, he must tell the DVLA [3].

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Let him give the full story; acknowledged the uncertainty he has been living with.
Who can come with him, driving, worry, practical support.
Picked up swallowing and “no pain at all” as significant cues and explored them.
Idea (something serious), concern (a serious cause), expectation (an explanation, even bad news).
Video observation of wasting, fasciculations, tongue and speech, plus the physiotherapist’s recorded UMN and LMN signs; further examination never delays referral.
MND versus cervical myelopathy, myasthenia, multifocal motor neuropathy, stroke and benign fasciculations.
Screened for choking, weight loss, chest infections and respiratory symptoms.
Stated that the pattern is serious and neurological without giving a diagnosis he cannot confirm.
Referral without delay, naming the possible diagnosis, with direct contact with the neurologist (NG42).
Swallow safety advice and driving advice; bloods not allowed to delay referral.
Clear triggers for faster review; follow-up after neurology; support offered.

social.t: He has been worrying on his own. Offer to include someone he trusts, and give him a way to reach the practice before the appointment.
Hand weakness and tripping affect work, driving and safety at home; occupational therapy and physiotherapy will be part of specialist care.

legal.t: Once MND is diagnosed, he must tell the DVLA; Group 1 drivers may keep driving if safe control is maintained, with licences reviewed periodically (DVLA). Until assessed, advise him not to drive if weakness affects safe control.
If MND is confirmed, advance decisions to refuse treatment and lasting power of attorney (Mental Capacity Act 2005) should be discussed early, while he can communicate easily.

professional.t: GMC Decision making and consent (2020) supports sharing information patients want. Answer direct questions honestly, and let the neurologist confirm the diagnosis (NG42).
Offer a follow-up after the neurology appointment, and code the suspected diagnosis so colleagues know the context.

community.t: The MND Association offers information and support for people being investigated, as well as after diagnosis.

redFlags: Choking on food or drink, weight loss, chest infections
Breathlessness lying flat, morning headaches, daytime sleepiness
psychosocial: Worry and how he is coping
Work, driving and safety at home
ice: Idea: something serious, since weakness without pain seems odd
Concern: fear of a serious cause
Expectation: an explanation, even if it is bad news

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: “The weakness, muscle thinning and twitching, with slurred speech and no pain or numbness, point to a problem with the nerves that control the muscles. It needs a neurologist urgently to find the cause.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Think of the nerves to your muscles as electrical wiring from the brain and spinal cord. The wiring for movement seems affected, while the wiring for feeling is working normally. A specialist needs to test the wiring to find out why.”

management.reflectIce: “You wanted an honest explanation. This is serious enough that I want a specialist to see you quickly, and I’ll tell them exactly what we’re looking for.”
management.psychosocial: Offer support, invite someone to the appointment, and advise on driving and swallowing safety.
sharedPlan: Neurology referral today naming the possible diagnosis, plus a phone call for urgency (NG42)
Routine bloods if needed, without delaying referral
safetyNet: Contact the practice at once for choking, chest infection, breathlessness or rapid worsening

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station tests whether you recognise a red-flag pattern without the usual cancer signs, and whether you can be honest under uncertainty. Candidates fail by reassuring, by delaying, or by announcing a diagnosis they cannot confirm.

items.fail: Attributing the symptoms to a trapped nerve, age or anxiety.
items.why: Progressive painless motor weakness with fasciculations and bulbar symptoms is a red flag.
items.fix: Name the pattern and refer urgently.

items.fail: Ordering tests and reviewing in a month before referring.
items.why: NG42: refer without delay; tests must not hold up referral.
items.fix: Refer today and phone the neurologist.

items.fail: Skipping the swallow and breathing questions.
items.why: Choking and respiratory weakness need faster action.
items.fix: Ask about choking, weight, chest infections, orthopnoea and morning headaches.

items.fail: Dodging the direct question about MND.
items.why: Evasion breaks trust and increases fear.
items.fix: “It’s one of the things being looked for. I can’t confirm it, and you’ll be seen quickly.”

items.why: NG42: the diagnosis should come from a neurologist, and mimics exist.
items.fix: Be honest about seriousness, not certain about the label.

items.why: Hand weakness and tripping affect safe driving and falls.
items.fix: Advise no driving until assessed, and DVLA notification if diagnosed.
